nodes.label: Router.scatterGatherFirstCompleted
nodes.rationale: Sends every message to all routees and answers the caller with the first reply; the losers keep running and their replies are discarded. This is the hedged-request pattern: it does not increase throughput, it lowers the tail - N routees each do the whole job, so you pay N times the work for the minimum of N latencies. It pays only when the slow tail is much slower than the median, and it is for idempotent READS: there is no cancel message, so N-fold work means N side effects.

nodes.label: ScatterGatherOptions
nodes.rationale: A builder or a plain { timeoutMs } object, both validated at the Router.scatterGatherFirstCompleted(...) call so the stack still points at the caller.

nodes.label: The reply contract
nodes.rationale: The router must intercept routee replies to pick a winner, so it needs a reply target: ask, or tell with an explicit sender. A bare tell has none, so nothing is scattered, the message is dropped and the router logs a warning rather than throwing - a throw would fail the router through supervision and the restart would take every other in-flight scatter down with it. The winning reply is attributed to the routee that produced it, which for hedged reads answers 'which replica won'.

nodes.label: AggregateError failure reporting
nodes.rationale: Every failure rejects with one AggregateError whose errors array holds one error per routee in scatter order. One type on purpose: a caller branching on the error TYPE to find out how many routees failed would learn nothing the errors array does not already carry. It survives the cluster wire because envelopes are framed as the tagged JSON tree, but members lose their classes - across nodes compare e.name rather than using instanceof.

nodes.label: withTimeoutMs (default 4500)
nodes.rationale: The deadline for one whole scatter, applied as the timeout on each routee's ask. The default sits just under ActorRef.ask's 5000 deliberately: the router can only report which routees failed after its own deadline passes, so a matching budget would leave the caller already timed out with an AskTimeoutError instead of the AggregateError this router exists to produce. In-flight routee asks are not cancelled when a scatter ends early.

nodes.label: Losing routees are not cancelled
nodes.source_location: ## What it buys, and what it costs
nodes.rationale: A routee that loses the race runs to completion and answers into a reply ref that has already been discarded.

nodes.label: Losing replies do not reach dead letters
nodes.rationale: A losing reply is addressed to the router's own one-shot reply ref, which is not an actor: once settled it drops what arrives, silently. Nothing shows in dead letters and no metric counts it, so measuring how often a routee loses means instrumenting the routee.

nodes.label: The fan-out is not awaited in the handler
nodes.rationale: The runtime awaits an actor's handler before dequeuing the next message, so an async onReceive around Promise.any would park the router's whole mailbox for the duration of one scatter - a single stalled routee would hold up every other caller for the full timeoutMs and concurrent asks would serialize. As written, hundreds of scatters overlap freely.

nodes.label: Scatter/gather metrics
nodes.rationale: router_scatter_gather_resolved_total (labelled first / timeout / all-failed / stopped / no-reply-target) and a latency histogram observing the WINNER's latency. timeout and all-failed are split because they call for different responses - too slow versus broken. Neither carries a router path, so several routers in one system aggregate and the log's actor path is what tells them apart.

nodes.label: postStop fails every open scatter
nodes.rationale: Rather than leaving the caller to discover the router is gone when the ask eventually times out. The routees are already stopped so their replies cannot arrive, and waiting out timeoutMs would make shutdown as slow as the longest configured deadline. A restart does the same, since preRestart defaults to postStop.
